title: Template Literal Types
summary: Describe strings by their pattern, build unions of names from other unions, and pull typed parameters out of route strings with infer.
intro: Plenty of strings in real code follow a pattern. Order IDs start with `ord_`, CSS sizes end in `px`, event names look like `order.created`, and routes look like `/orders/:orderId`. A template literal type writes that pattern as a type, with the same backtick syntax as a template string. In this lesson you check strings against patterns, build unions of names from other unions, and read the parameters out of a route string at the type level, the way typed routers do.

practice.title: Order IDs
practice.prompt:
Order IDs in this shop start with `ord_`. Type them with a pattern, and build a link only for strings that pass the check.

1. Export `type OrderId` as a template literal type: `ord_` followed by any text.
2. Export `isOrderId(s: string): s is OrderId`, which returns `true` when `s` starts with `ord_`.
3. `orderUrl(id: OrderId)` is done. For each string in `inputs`, print its URL when it's an order ID, or `not an order id` when it isn't.
4. Keep `export`: hidden type tests import your names, and Check also runs your functions on other strings.

Expected output:

```text
https://example.com/orders/ord_1001
not an order id
https://example.com/orders/ord_2002
```

tests.output:
https://example.com/orders/ord_1001
not an order id
https://example.com/orders/ord_2002

https://example.com/orders/ord_1001
not an order id
https://example.com/orders/ord_2002
https://example.com/orders/ord_77
not an order id
not an order id

typeTests.imports: import { isOrderId, orderUrl, type OrderId } from "./main.ts";

cases.name: a checked string is an order id

hints: Write the pattern the way the examples write `UserId` and `Hex`: the fixed text, then `${string}` for the rest, all between backticks.
`s.startsWith("ord_")` is the whole check. The return type `s is OrderId` is what narrows `input` in the loop.
In the loop, print `isOrderId(input) ? orderUrl(input) : "not an order id"`.

practice.title: Permission strings
practice.prompt:
An admin panel checks permissions written as a resource, a colon, and an access level. Build every permission from two unions, and check what a clerk may do.

1. Export `type Permission`, a template literal type built from `"orders" | "products"`, a colon, and `"read" | "write"`.
2. Export `can(perms: readonly Permission[], p: Permission): boolean`, which returns `true` when `perms` includes `p`.
3. For each permission in `checks`, print `<permission> is allowed` or `<permission> is denied` for the clerk.
4. Keep `export`: hidden type tests import your names, and Check also calls `can` with other permissions.

Expected output:

```text
orders:read is allowed
orders:write is denied
products:write is allowed
```

tests.output:
orders:read is allowed
orders:write is denied
products:write is allowed

tests.append:
const viewer: Permission[] = ["orders:read"];
console.log(can(viewer, "products:read"), can(viewer, "orders:read"), can([], "orders:write"));
tests.output:
orders:read is allowed
orders:write is denied
products:write is allowed
false true false

hints: Give each union its own `${...}` placeholder with a colon between them, like `EventName` in the first example.
Loop over `checks`, and build each line with a template string: the permission, then `is`, then `allowed` or `denied`.

steps.title: Route parameters with infer

examples.title: One parameter
examples.prompt: Pull the name out of a route segment like `:orderId`, at the type level and at run time.
examples.output:
orders is fixed text
:orderId is the parameter orderId
examples.explanation: In `ParamName`, the pattern is a colon followed by `infer P`. A segment that starts with a colon matches, and `P` is the rest of it. `"orders"` has no colon, so the false branch gives `never`, the empty union. `paramName` applies the same rule to values at run time, with `startsWith` and `slice`. The type and the function follow one rule, one for the checker and one for the program.

examples.title: All parameters
examples.prompt: Collect every parameter name of a route pattern with a recursive type, and list the same names at run time.
examples.explanation: Follow `"/orders/:orderId/items/:itemId"` through the type. The first pattern matches: `${string}` skips `/orders/`, `Param` is `orderId`, the text up to the next `/`, and `Rest` is `items/:itemId`. The type then runs again on `Rest`. No `/` follows `itemId`, so the first pattern fails there and the second one matches, giving `itemId`. The result is the union of both names. `/health` has no colon, so neither pattern matches, and the result is `never`. `paramNames` finds the same names at run time.

examples.title: A typed path builder
examples.prompt: OpenAPI writes path parameters in braces, like `/orders/{orderId}/items/{itemId}`. Fill in such a path with a function whose type says which values a call must pass, and leave one out.
examples.output: main.ts(16,58): error TS2741: Property 'itemId' is missing in type '{ orderId: string; }' but required in type 'Record<"itemId" | "orderId", string>'.

practice.title: Typed URL builder
practice.prompt:
Express writes route parameters as `:name`. Write `buildPath`, which fills in a route's parameters and only accepts calls that pass every one of them. 1. The starter has `ExtractParams`, the recursive type from the examples. Change `buildPath` to `buildPath

(pattern: P, params: Record, string>): string`. 2. Replace each segment that starts with `:` by the value for its name, and keep every other segment as it is. 3. Read `params` through a `Record` variable, so you need no cast. Check rejects `as`. 4. Keep `export`: hidden type tests import `buildPath`, and Check also builds other paths. Expected output: ```text /users/42 /orders/ord_1001/items/3 ```

cases.name: rejects a call without its params
accepts every param
cases.code: const path: string = buildPath("/users/:id/posts/:postId", { id: "1", postId: "2" });

cases.name: rejects a param the route doesn't have
a route without params takes an empty object

hints: Follow `fillPath` from the last example: the same generic signature, with `ExtractParams` in place of `PathParams`.
Start the body with `const values: Record<string, string> = params;`. Then `values[name]` is allowed for any string `name`, and it's `string | undefined`.
Split the pattern on `/`, map each segment that starts with `:` to `values[segment.slice(1)] ?? segment`, and join the segments with `/` again.

recap: - A template literal type, written between backticks like a template string, describes strings by a pattern. `${string}` matches any text, even none, and `${number}` matches text that reads as a number. - A literal fits when it matches the pattern. A plain `string` needs a type guard first. - A union inside a template makes one string per member, and several unions make every combination. - `Uppercase`, `Lowercase`, `Capitalize`, and `Uncapitalize` change the case of string types, never of values. - `infer` in a pattern pulls out a piece of a string type, and a type that refers to itself in a conditional branch can walk a whole string. - `Record, string>` makes a function demand exactly the parameters its pattern names. Read it through a `Record` variable instead of casting.
